name: Socotra

pin.note: Approximate centre of Socotra main island

creatures.iucn_status: Vulnerable (VU); 2022 assessment per Wikipedia; GBIF confirms VU
creatures.status_note: Endemic to Socotra; about 250-500 mature individuals, declining; described in 2010.

facts.statement: Socotra lies south of the Arabian Peninsula and east of the Horn of Africa, centred at roughly 12.51 N, 53.92 E.
facts.evidence_note: Geography section gives position and coordinates.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: NASA describes Socotra as an archipelago at the eastern end of the Gulf of Aden, about 320 km (200 mi) south of the Yemeni mainland.
facts.evidence_note: Location paragraph of the Earth Observatory image caption.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Britannica puts Socotra roughly 340 km (210 mi) southeast of Yemen and calls it the largest of several islands stretching east from the Horn of Africa.
facts.evidence_note: Opening description of the island.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: UNESCO describes the World Heritage property as four main islands plus two rocky islets, forming an archipelago about 250 km long in the northwest Indian Ocean.
facts.source_title: Socotra Archipelago - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Property description on the listing page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The island has a tropical desert climate with generally sparse rain, and long droughts can occur.
facts.evidence_note: Climate remark in the NASA caption.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: At Socotra airport the mean annual temperature is about 28 C, with a recorded high of 40.6 C and low of 17.0 C.
facts.evidence_note: Climate summary figures in the article.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Rainfall at the airport averages about 193 mm per year, while upland areas can receive around 800 mm annually.
facts.evidence_note: Climate section rainfall figures.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The northeast monsoon (October-December) delivers most of the island's rain, whereas the southwest monsoon (June-September) brings strong winds and rough seas.
facts.evidence_note: Climate section describing monsoon seasons.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Cyclone Chapala passed just north of Socotra on 1 November 2015, the island's first hurricane-force impact since 1922, destroying about 237 homes and displacing roughly 18,000 people.
facts.evidence_note: Impact section of the Chapala article.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The main island of Socotra covers about 3,665 km2 and measures roughly 125-132 km long by 42-50 km wide, depending on the figure cited.
facts.evidence_note: Geography section dimensions.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Socotra's highest point is Mashanig in the Hajhir Mountains at about 1,503 m.
facts.evidence_note: Geography section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A tourism-sector geology page names Jebel Skand, above 1,550 m, as the archipelago's highest point, which differs from the 1,503 m figure for Mashanig.
facts.evidence_note: Description of the igneous highlands.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Limestone plateaus covering much of the island sit mostly at about 300-700 m and show karst features such as pavements, gullies and many caves, with few surface streams.
facts.evidence_note: Limestone plateau section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Socotra is continental in origin rather than volcanic, having split from the ancient supercontinent Gondwana.
facts.evidence_note: Geology remark in the NASA caption.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Arabia separated from Africa roughly 20-15 million years ago, opening the Gulf of Aden, with Socotra remaining on the African plate.
facts.evidence_note: Separation section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Hoq Cave, about 1.5 km inland on the northeast coast, holds inscriptions in six scripts, including Brahmi, Greek and Ethiopic Ge'ez, dating from the 1st to 6th centuries CE.
facts.evidence_note: Inscriptions and dates sections.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Portuguese forces took the port of Suq in 1507 and left in 1511 because of famine and disease.
facts.evidence_note: History section, Portuguese period. Re-checked 2026-10-09: no primary source confirmed it. Wikipedia and a CAPAsia essay agree on 1507 occupation, 1511 abandonment and hunger and disease, but the essay's publisher authority and the 'port of Suq' detail were not confirmed.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Mahra Sultanate was abolished in 1967 and Socotra joined South Yemen on 30 November 1967; it became part of unified Yemen in 1990.
facts.evidence_note: History section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Socotra Archipelago Biosphere Reserve was designated in 2003, Detwah Lagoon became a Ramsar site in 2007, and the archipelago became a World Heritage Site in 2008.
facts.source_title: Nature and people in the Socotra Archipelago
facts.evidence_note: Biosphere Reserve section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Socotra was separated from Hadhramaut Governorate to become its own Yemeni governorate in December 2013, with Hadibu as capital.
facts.evidence_note: Creation and status paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The most recent census cited by UNESCO estimated about 100,000 people across the archipelago, and the island holds roughly 480,000 domestic goats.
facts.source_title: Nature and people in the Socotra Archipelago
facts.evidence_note: Population and livelihoods sections.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Soqotri, an unwritten Modern South Arabian Semitic language, is spoken mainly on the Socotra archipelago and is classified by UNESCO as severely endangered.
facts.evidence_note: Language family and status paragraphs.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: According to Wikipedia, the UAE took control of the airport and seaport in April 2018, returned them to Yemen in a May 2018 deal, and the Southern Transitional Council seized the archipelago in June 2020, holding it until January 2026.
facts.evidence_note: Recent political situation section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: UNESCO records 825 plant species on the archipelago, about 37% endemic, plus 34 reptile species (about 90% endemic) and 96 land snail species (about 95% endemic).
facts.source_title: Socotra Archipelago - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Biodiversity description.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: UNESCO lists 192 bird species for the archipelago, of which 44 breed and 85 are regular migrants, with 22 BirdLife Important Bird Areas.
facts.source_title: Socotra Archipelago - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Bird figures.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The surrounding waters hold 253 reef-building coral species and 730 coastal fish species.
facts.source_title: Socotra Archipelago - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Marine biodiversity figures.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The largest remaining stands of dragon's blood trees (Dracaena cinnabari) are on Socotra, though goats threaten them.
facts.evidence_note: Vegetation paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: UNESCO lists current pressures as road building, overgrazing and overharvesting of land and marine resources, with tourism and invasive species as future risks.
facts.source_title: Socotra Archipelago - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Threats section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Projections cited for the dragon's blood tree suggest a 45 percent habitat loss by 2080, while goats browse seedlings; the tree is rated Vulnerable.
facts.evidence_note: Threats and status sections.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Invasive rats and cats are increasing on Socotra and threaten native plants and animals.
facts.evidence_note: Introduced species section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: UNESCO says all component areas have legal protection and about 75% of the land is protected, but legislation, management capacity and enforcement need strengthening.
facts.source_title: Socotra Archipelago - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Conservation and management section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Socotra buzzard (Buteo socotraensis) occurs only on Socotra, Yemen.
facts.evidence_note: Endemism line.
facts.subject: socotra-buzzard

facts.statement: GBIF's Backbone lists Buteo socotraensis with an IUCN Red List category of Vulnerable (VU); the response gives no year.
facts.source_title: GBIF IUCN Red List category: Buteo socotraensis
facts.evidence_note: IUCN category field.
facts.subject: socotra-buzzard

facts.statement: The 2022 IUCN Red List assessment, as reported by Wikipedia, rates the Socotra buzzard Vulnerable with about 250-500 mature individuals and a declining population.
facts.evidence_note: Conservation status section.
facts.subject: socotra-buzzard

facts.statement: The Socotra buzzard was formally described as a new species in 2010 by R. F. Porter and G. M. Kirwan in the Bulletin of the British Ornithologists' Club.
facts.source_title: Socotra Buzzard declared separate species from Common
facts.evidence_note: Article on the formal description.
facts.subject: socotra-buzzard

facts.statement: Socotra buzzards live in foothills, plateaus and deep ravines, usually at 150-800 m, and need cliffs for nesting.
facts.evidence_note: Habitat description.
facts.subject: socotra-buzzard

facts.statement: With few mammals on the island, the buzzard feeds mainly on reptiles and invertebrates, hunting opportunistically.
facts.evidence_note: Diet description.
facts.subject: socotra-buzzard

facts.statement: The buzzard may compete with vultures, ravens and falcons for nesting cliffs.
facts.evidence_note: Threats and competition remark.
facts.subject: socotra-buzzard

facts.statement: GBIF holds 185 occurrence records for Buteo socotraensis, 181 of them from Yemen.
facts.source_title: GBIF occurrence search: Buteo socotraensis by country
facts.evidence_note: Country facet counts.
facts.subject: socotra-buzzard

facts.statement: The Egyptian vulture (Neophron percnopterus) population on Socotra was estimated at about 1,900 birds, probably equal to roughly 800 pairs, and the authors say the species was given Globally Endangered status in 2007 while the Socotra population appears healthy.
facts.source_title: The Egyptian Vulture Neophron percnopterus on Socotra, Yemen: population, ecology, conservation and ethno-ornithology
facts.publisher: Sandgrouse (Ornithological Society of the Middle East)
facts.evidence_note: Population and Conservation sections (Porter & Suleiman, Sandgrouse 34, 2012). Several counting methods gave 1,600-2,300; only 15-20% of the island was covered per visit, so the figure is an estimate.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Socotra cormorant (Phalacrocorax nigrogularis) is rated Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (listed since 2000, per Wikipedia) because of few breeding localities and ongoing rapid decline; breeding on Socotra itself was only confirmed in 2005 despite the name.
facts.evidence_note: Status, Breeding and Distribution paragraphs. Wikipedia reports the IUCN rating; the IUCN page was not read. Its main range is the Persian Gulf and SE Arabian coast.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Porter and Suleiman (2016) report that the islet of Kal Farun (Kal Farun IBA, Socotra archipelago) holds about 2,500 pairs of Socotra cormorant (Phalacrocorax nigrogularis), over 2% of the global population, and list the species as globally vulnerable.
facts.source_title: The Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas of the Socotra archipelago, Yemen
facts.publisher: Sandgrouse (Ornithological Society of the Middle East)
facts.evidence_note: Site account for Kal Farun (IBA 20) and Table 1 of the paper; the same paper notes rats and possibly cats might threaten nesting seabirds but this has not been assessed.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Socotra bunting (Emberiza socotrana), endemic to Socotra, is listed as globally vulnerable with a population estimate of about 3,800 in a 2016 survey paper, which also reports fewer than 20 pairs at Jabal Ma'alah, more than 1% of the global population.
facts.source_title: The Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas of the Socotra archipelago, Yemen
facts.publisher: Sandgrouse (Ornithological Society of the Middle East)
facts.evidence_note: Table 1 (population and 2016 Red List status) and Jabal Ma'alah (IBA 2) account. Scientific name taken from the Wikipedia bunting page; the table units are as tabulated. Wikipedia gives Near Threatened, see next fact.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wikipedia lists the Socotra bunting (Emberiza socotrana) as Near Threatened (IUCN 3.1), endemic to Socotra, with habitat loss as a threat to its high-altitude shrubland habitat.
facts.evidence_note: Infobox and text. This differs from the Vulnerable listing in the 2016 Sandgrouse paper, so the two are recorded separately; the more recent assessment was not verified.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Socotra grosbeak (Rhynchostruthus socotranus) is found only on Socotra and is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN per Wikipedia, with about 6,500 adult individuals living from mountains to sea level in dry scrub or woodland of Euphorbia, Acacia and Juniperus.
facts.evidence_note: Status, population and habitat text. The 2016 Sandgrouse paper estimates about 17,000 for the same bird, so population figures differ between sources.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Socotra chameleon (Chamaeleo monachus) is endemic to Socotra and listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN per Wikipedia, living in dense shrubland, dry wadis and sometimes palm plantations.
facts.evidence_note: Infobox and habitat text; Wikipedia adds the species is endangered by overgrazing, which is a threat, not a formal category. No population figure given.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Mongabay reports that, according to the IUCN, nine of the island's endemic frankincense species (Boswellia) are closer to extinction, with Boswellia nana moving from Vulnerable to Critically Endangered and B. elongata, B. ameero, B. bullata, B. dioscoridis and B. popoviana moving to Endangered since 2004.
facts.source_title: Iconic frankincense trees of Yemen's Socotra Island have become rarer
facts.evidence_note: Body of the news article; 11 of the 24 known Boswellia species are Socotra-only. Secondary report of an IUCN assessment that was not read directly.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Nesting loggerhead turtles (Caretta caretta) at Abalhen Beach on Socotra fell from 206 individuals in 2007 to 95 in 2012, and the submission lists the loggerhead as endangered and on CITES Appendix I.
facts.source_title: Template for submission of scientific and technical information to describe EBSAs: Yemen (Socotra), ebsaws-2015-02
facts.evidence_note: Turtle section of the Yemen submission to the CBD EBSA workshop; the author calls Abalhen the country's most important loggerhead nesting area and blames poaching and road disturbance. Title paraphrased from the file name.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Ramsar sheet for Detwah Lagoon on Socotra describes the leopard stingray (Himantura uarnak) as vulnerable and the bluespotted ribbontail ray (Taeniura lymma) as near-threatened, noting it is the only site on the island where both were recorded.
facts.source_title: Detwah Lagoon - Ramsar Sites Information Service (Site no. 1736)
facts.evidence_note: Species section of the Ramsar Information Sheet. Status wording is the sheet's own; Wikipedia calls the first ray the reticulate whipray.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Coral reefs cover about 130 km2 off the sheltered north coast of Socotra island and nearly 45 km2 around its southern coasts, roughly 175 km2 in total.
facts.source_title: Nature and people in the Socotra Archipelago
facts.evidence_note: Marine and coral section of the UNESCO document; read via text extraction of the first 100,000 characters.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: In May 1998, during El Nino, sea-surface temperature in Socotra's waters reached 32 C, and the resulting coral bleaching doubled the share of dead coral on the reefs from 8% to 16%; effects of the 2014-2017 global bleaching event there have not been studied.
facts.source_title: Nature and people in the Socotra Archipelago
facts.evidence_note: Sea temperature and coral bleaching passage in the later part of the document (offset 100000 fetch).
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Socotra's marine area totals 1,816,200 ha in the biosphere reserve, split into a 166,800 ha core zone and a 1,649,800 ha buffer, and the 27 Marine Nature Sanctuaries cover 154 km2; Socotra was also listed as an Ecologically or Biologically Significant Marine Area in 2016.
facts.source_title: Nature and people in the Socotra Archipelago
facts.evidence_note: Protected-areas passage of the UNESCO document; zoning plan dated 2000.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: In the summer monsoon the Great Whirl, an anticyclonic eddy 400-600 km across, typically sits at 5-10 N, 52-57 E and about 200 km southwest of the Socotra Gyre, and water transport south of Socotra island peaks at 60-70 Sv.
facts.evidence_note: Great Whirl and Socotra passages. Regional ocean circulation, not Socotra-specific measurements; the page's upwelling figures refer to the Somali coast and were not used.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Detwah Lagoon on Socotra covers 580 ha as a coastal lagoon with a tidal inlet to the sea, bordered by sand dunes, and its relatively pristine seagrass beds shelter and feed juvenile fish.
facts.source_title: Detwah Lagoon - Ramsar Sites Information Service (Site no. 1736)
facts.evidence_note: Site description. The sheet gives no salinity, depth or temperature figures.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Socotra's traditional water sources are kareefs, which are cemented rainwater cisterns, and dug wells, fed by periodic monsoon rain and permanent highland fog, and the document notes wells and reservoirs are increasingly being dug with unknown long-term effects.
facts.source_title: Nature and people in the Socotra Archipelago
facts.evidence_note: Freshwater passage of the UNESCO document.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Plastic litter accumulates in the wadis and on the beaches of the Socotra archipelago, and the document also lists solid waste as a major challenge.
facts.source_title: Nature and people in the Socotra Archipelago
facts.evidence_note: Threats passages (later part of document); no plastic quantities are given.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: At Socotra Airport the annual mean daily maximum is 30.8 C and mean daily minimum 25.1 C, with about 21.7 rainy days a year and average relative humidity of 65%, ranging from 57% in August to 73% in December.
facts.evidence_note: Climate section and climate table. Complements the existing airport temperature and rainfall facts.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Cyclone Chapala brought more than 410 mm of rain to the normally arid western side of Socotra in November 2015.
facts.evidence_note: Climate section. Single secondary source; island-wide totals are not given on the Chapala page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Cyclone Megh passed just north of Socotra on 8 November 2015, a week after Chapala, with estimated 1-minute winds of 205 km/h from JTWC, killing 18 people on the island and destroying about 500 homes.
facts.evidence_note: Socotra impact section; IMD gave 175 km/h 3-minute winds. Also about 80% of roads were impassable and wells contaminated.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Cyclone Mekunu passed east of Socotra on 23 May 2018, killing at least 20 people there, prompting evacuation of over 1,000 households and capsizing 120 fishing boats.
facts.evidence_note: Impacts on Socotra section. The page gives no Socotra rainfall or wind figures (its 617 mm is for Salalah, Oman).
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A 2001-era planning lecture on Socotra places the north-east monsoon at October to April and the south-west monsoon at May to September, quotes annual rainfall of 170 mm from northern coastal readings, and reports about 630 mm in 22 days in late 1999.
facts.evidence_note: Climate section of the article; author calls mountain rainfall of up to 1,000 mm speculation. Monsoon dates differ from Wikipedia (NE monsoon October-December), and data are dated.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wet refugia on Socotra, such as cliffs and escarpments with extra rain and mist, hold species twice as likely to be endemic as elsewhere on the island, and the Hajhir massif has 55 endemic species found only in that refugium.
facts.evidence_note: Ecology and refugia text.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: About 71% of mammal species on Socotra are non-native, as the island has no native mammals except a few insectivores, and introduced animals include goats, sheep, cows, camels, donkeys, cats, rats, mice and one civet species.
facts.source_title: Nature and people in the Socotra Archipelago
facts.evidence_note: Introduced species passage of the UNESCO document.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Because Socotra has no dogs, Egyptian vultures are the top scavenger at rubbish dumps and carcasses, feeding on discarded food scraps, fish remains at the Hadibu fish souk beach and road-killed animals.
facts.source_title: The Egyptian Vulture Neophron percnopterus on Socotra, Yemen: population, ecology, conservation and ethno-ornithology
facts.publisher: Sandgrouse (Ornithological Society of the Middle East)
facts.evidence_note: Feeding section; the largest recorded gathering was 175 birds at a wedding feast on 3 March 2011.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Socotra holds over 1,560 insect taxa with over 660 endemic, 645 beetle species of which 47% are endemic, and about 100 land snail species of which 98% are endemic.
facts.source_title: Nature and people in the Socotra Archipelago
facts.evidence_note: Endemism data in the UNESCO document; the UNESCO World Heritage page gives 96 land snail species and 95% endemic, so counts differ between sources.
facts.subject: island

gaps: IUCN Red List and BirdLife pages could not be fetched, so the 2022 assessment year rests on Wikipedia; GBIF confirms category only
No authoritative coordinates for the island on UNESCO page
Official recent population figure for the main island not verified
History coverage is thinner than targeted (4 facts); Periplus, Hoq Cave discovery and 1834 British episode were fetched but not retained
conflicts: Highest peak: 1,503 m Mashanig (Wikipedia) vs over 1,550 m Jebel Skand (welcometosocotra.com)
Distance from Yemen mainland: about 320 km (NASA) vs about 340 km (Britannica)
Plant species count: 825 (UNESCO) vs 835 (Wikipedia Flora of Socotra; not used)
Population: about 100,000 archipelago (UNESCO) vs 50,000-60,000 main island (Wikipedia, not used)
